summary: Defines which cryptographic algorithms must be implemented for ESP and AH, so that at least one common choice exists between any two implementations. It also lists algorithms that should be implemented because they may become mandatory. It is a standards-track document that was later replaced by RFC 4835.

plainLanguage.summary: Two strangers need at least one language in common. This memo lists the secret languages every IPsec product must know.

subtitle: Which encryption and authentication algorithms every IPsec ESP and AH implementation must, should or may support.

tldr.problem: Two IPsec implementations can only talk if they share at least one algorithm, and the right algorithms change as cryptography is attacked and improved.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC lists mandatory-to-implement and recommended algorithms for ESP and AH in tables, using MUST, SHOULD and extra levels such as SHOULD+ and MUST-, outside the protocol specifications themselves.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes the algorithm requirements in RFC 2402 and RFC 2406, and it has itself been obsoleted by RFC 4835.

today: RFC 4305 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4835, which now holds these requirements. It replaced the algorithm requirements of RFC 2402 and RFC 2406.

sections.title: Why a Separate Requirements Document
sections.content:
The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and the Authentication Header (AH) protect data sent over an IPsec Security Association (SA). To ensure interoperability, the specifications must name a set of mandatory-to-implement algorithms so that at least one algorithm is available in all implementations.

The RFC points out that algorithms are attacked continuously, so the mandatory choice should be conservative, and performance matters because many IPsec uses are performance sensitive. Because the mandatory set may need to change, it is deliberately kept out of the main IPsec, ESP and AH specifications (RFC 4301, RFC 4303, RFC 4302). Only this document should need updating when the choice changes.

The document also tries to name algorithms that may become mandatory later, with no guarantee that they will.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules of the secret language club change over time, so they are written on a separate card. When the rules change, only that card gets replaced.

sections.title: Requirement Levels
sections.content:
The usual RFC 2119 keywords apply (RFC 2119). The RFC adds three more, each meaning the same as the base word but with a hint about the future:

  • SHOULD+: like SHOULD, but likely to be promoted to MUST in the future.
  • SHOULD-: like SHOULD, but likely to be deprecated to a MAY or worse in a future version.
  • MUST-: like MUST, but at some point the algorithm is expected to stop being a MUST.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides plain must and should, there are signs saying: this one will probably become a must soon, or this one will probably be dropped soon.

sections.title: Algorithm Requirements for ESP and AH
sections.content:
Which algorithms a given SA actually uses is decided by a negotiation mechanism such as IKE or by pre-establishment. Additional standard and proprietary algorithms may be implemented beyond those listed.

For ESP encryption, NULL is a MUST and TripleDES-CBC is MUST-. AES-CBC with 128-bit keys is SHOULD+, AES-CTR is SHOULD, and DES-CBC is SHOULD NOT. For ESP authentication, HMAC-SHA1-96 and NULL are both MUST, AES-XCBC-MAC-96 is SHOULD+ and HMAC-MD5-96 is MAY.

Because ESP encryption and authentication are each optional, both NULL algorithms are required for consistency with how services are negotiated. However, encryption and authentication MUST NOT both be NULL.

For AH, which only authenticates, HMAC-SHA1-96 is MUST, AES-XCBC-MAC-96 is SHOULD+ and HMAC-MD5-96 is MAY. The RFC notes that weaknesses have become apparent in MD5 but should not affect its use with HMAC.

No combined-mode algorithm (one providing both confidentiality and authentication) is suggested or required yet, though AES-CCM, preferred for IEEE 802.11 security, is expected to be of interest soon.
sections.plainLanguage: Every product must know the do-nothing option and the older triple scrambler, and must know a particular signing method. It should learn the newer scramblers, and it should not offer the old weak one.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2402 and RFC 2406
sections.content:
The old AH and ESP specifications (RFC 2402 and RFC 2406) carried their own algorithm requirements. Their replacements no longer do, and this document supplies them for both protocols.

Three requirements change. Single DES (DES-CBC) goes from MUST to SHOULD NOT. HMAC-MD5-96 goes from MUST to MAY. HMAC-SHA1-96 stays MUST.

The RFC notes that the IETF had deprecated single DES years earlier, but this is the first standards-track recognition of that, and that NIST proposed withdrawing single DES as a US Government standard in a 26 July 2004 notice. Triple DES remains approved by both the IETF and NIST.
sections.plainLanguage: The old weak scrambler used to be required and now should be avoided. The old signing method that was required is now only optional.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security depends on both the strength of the algorithms and keys and on the engineering and administration of the protocol around them. This document is only about choosing mandatory-to-implement algorithms.

The algorithms marked MUST or SHOULD are not known to be broken and are believed likely to stay secure for the foreseeable future, but not necessarily forever. The RFC therefore expects new revisions to be issued from time to time to reflect current best practice.
sections.plainLanguage: A lock is only as good as its key and how people use it. Today's good locks may be picked tomorrow, so the list will be updated.
